title: The demo worked because every incident followed the template.
body:
The demo worked because every incident followed the template. Real SRE traffic didn't.

The POC was clean: ~20 users, incidents that mostly matched the structured format. My retrieval and resolution-step generation leaned on that structure — pull the right fields, ground the LLM, surface the similar incident.

Then it met 200+ SREs and years of real ServiceNow history. Teams hadn't filled the incident format consistently — fields skipped, freeform where I expected structure, structure where there wasn't any. The assumptions that made the notebook version look smart were the exact thing buckling at scale.

The fix wasn't a better parser. I went back through the actual data, found ~6-month windows where teams had genuinely been consistent, anchored on those, and designed the pipeline to tolerate the drift instead of pretending it away.

A notebook proves the idea works on the data you picked. Real traffic tells you which of your assumptions were load-bearing.
longform:
## The assumption I didn't know I was making

The incident-resolution assistant started as a ~20-user POC. In the notebook it looked sharp: pull the structured fields off each incident, ground the model, surface the nearest past incident and its resolution steps. Every incident I tested followed the ServiceNow format, so parsing the structure was free. The load-bearing assumption I never wrote down: that the structure would hold.

## What broke at scale

Then it met 200+ SREs and years of real ServiceNow history. People hadn't filled the format consistently — fields skipped, freeform where I expected tags, structure where the template didn't ask for any.

The retrieval layer had its own version of the problem. Similar-incident search ran on embeddings, and on this data everything looked alike — same product vocabulary, same log-line cadence — so "nearest" stopped meaning "similar." That's not just my bad luck: **Steck, Ekanadham & Kallus** (Netflix, WWW 2024) show cosine similarity between embeddings can be *arbitrary and therefore meaningless*, because the regularization used to train a model silently shapes the geometry you're measuring [1]. On a homogeneous corpus that effect is amplified — everything is close to everything.

## The fix wasn't a better parser

Two things moved the numbers. I masked the identifiers dominating the vectors — region, timestamp, host — so the model stopped keying on boilerplate. Then I stopped asking embeddings to do the whole job: hybrid retrieval, BM25 for the exact tokens and vectors for the semantics, combined. A standard, calibration-free way to fuse two ranked lists like that is **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** (Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) [2]. Similar-incident recall went from ~30% to 80%+.

For the structure problem, I didn't try to reform an org's incident habits. I found the ~6-month windows where teams had been consistent, anchored there, and designed the pipeline to tolerate the drift instead of pretending it away.

## The lesson, already written down

A notebook proves the idea works on the data you picked. Production is other people's formatting — it tells you which of your assumptions were load-bearing. This gap has a name: **Sculley et al.'s** *Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems* (NIPS 2015) catalogs exactly these failure modes — data dependencies, *changes in the external world*, boundary erosion — as the ongoing cost a slick POC hides [3].

None of the fixes were clever. The work was finding the pockets of order already in the mess and building on those.
